subChunks.title: Forms: Validation and Multi-Field Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: Single-field forms are straightforward. Real forms have five, ten, twenty fields — and they need validation, error messages, and submission state. The patterns you use for multi-field forms determine whether your code stays manageable or collapses under its own weight.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Managing multi-field state with an object

function RegistrationForm() {
  const [fields, setFields] = useState({
    username: '',
    email: '',
    password: '',
  });

  function handleChange(e) {
    const { name, value } = e.target;
    setFields(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: value }));
  }

  return (
    <form>
      <input name="username" value={fields.username} onChange={handleChange} />
      <input name="email"    value={fields.email}    onChange={handleChange} />
      <input name="password" value={fields.password} onChange={handleChange} type="password" />
    </form>
  );
}

Validate on submit

const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

function validate(fields) {
  const errs = {};
  if (!fields.username.trim()) errs.username = 'Username is required';
  if (!fields.email.includes('@')) errs.email = 'Enter a valid email';
  if (fields.password.length < 8) errs.password = 'At least 8 characters';
  return errs;
}

function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const errs = validate(fields);
  if (Object.keys(errs).length > 0) { setErrors(errs); return; }
  // Proceed
}

Validate on blur

function handleBlur(e) {
  const { name, value } = e.target;
  const fieldError = validateField(name, value);
  setErrors(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: fieldError }));
}

Submission state

const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);

async function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  if (submitting) return;
  setSubmitting(true);
  try {
    await registerUser(fields);
    navigate('/welcome');
  } catch (err) {
    setSubmitError(err.message);
  } finally {
    setSubmitting(false);
  }
}

<button type="submit" disabled={submitting}>
  {submitting ? 'Creating account...' : 'Create Account'}
</button>

Vex: "Disable the submit button while submitting. A double-submitted registration creates two accounts. A form that shows no feedback looks broken. Both cost you users."

useRef for uncontrolled inputs

import { useRef } from 'react';

function SimpleSearch() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    console.log(inputRef.current.value);
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input ref={inputRef} type="text" />
      <button type="submit">Search</button>
    </form>
  );
}

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: One useState per field is fine for two fields. For ten fields it is noise. Store all field values in one state object — the field's name attribute is the key. One handleChange function updates any field by reading e.target.name.

storyBeats.speaker: One handleChange for all fields

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Build a <LoginForm onSubmit /> with two fields: email and password. Use a single state object and single handler. Validate on submit: email must contain @, password min 6 chars. Show inline errors in <p data-testid="error-email"> and <p data-testid="error-password">. Call onSubmit(fields) if valid.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <RegistrationForm> from scratch with three fields: username (min 3 chars), email (must contain @), password (min 8 chars). Single state object, single handler. Show inline validation errors. Disable submit while submitting. Log fields on success.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the pattern of storing all form fields in one state object with a shared handleChange. Why is this preferable to a separate useState per field? Walk through what happens when a user types into the email input.

questions.prompt: In the single-object form state pattern, how does one `handleChange` function update the correct field?
options: It reads `e.target.name` and uses it as a computed property key: `[name]: value`
It reads `e.target.id` and finds the matching state key by ID
React automatically maps onChange events to the matching state key
It updates all fields simultaneously and React diffs to find the changed one
questions.answer: It reads `e.target.name` and uses it as a computed property key: `[name]: value`
questions.explanation: const { name, value } = e.target gives you the input's name and new value. setFields(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: value })) spreads existing fields and overwrites only the matching key.

questions.prompt: Why should the submit button be disabled while a form submission is in progress?
options: To prevent double-submissions — a second click would trigger a second async request
Disabled buttons look more professional in loading states
React throws an error if state is updated on an unmounted component after double-submit
The browser reloads the page if a submit event fires twice
questions.answer: To prevent double-submissions — a second click would trigger a second async request
questions.explanation: If the user clicks Submit twice before the async request completes, two identical requests go out. For actions like creating an account or placing an order, this creates duplicate records.

questions.prompt: When is `useRef` for an uncontrolled input preferable over `useState`?
options: When you only need the value at submission time and have no real-time validation or derived UI
When the form has more than 5 fields — useRef performs better at scale
When the input value might be empty — useState can't represent empty strings
useRef is always preferable — controlled inputs cause unnecessary re-renders
questions.answer: When you only need the value at submission time and have no real-time validation or derived UI
questions.explanation: Controlled inputs re-render on every keystroke — which is exactly what you need for live validation. If you don't need any of that, useRef reads the value once at submission with no state overhead.

questions.prompt: Validate-on-submit vs validate-on-blur: which is more appropriate for a long registration form?
options: Validate on blur for individual fields combined with a full validate-on-submit pass as the final gate
Validate on submit only — blur validation is too aggressive
Validate on every keystroke — gives the most immediate feedback
Validate on blur only — on-submit validation is redundant
questions.answer: Validate on blur for individual fields combined with a full validate-on-submit pass as the final gate
questions.explanation: Blur validation shows errors after the user finishes a field, which feels natural. A final on-submit pass catches fields the user skipped entirely. The combination gives good UX without being aggressive.
